implementation_notes: Default std-only realization: a static OnceLock holding a RwLock<HashMap<&str, Factory>>, reached through a registry() accessor that get_or_init's it; registration takes a write lock, lookup a read lock. LazyLock (Rust 1.80) is the same thing with an initializer expression and no accessor boilerplate.
pitfalls: A panicking writer poisons the RwLock and every later read().unwrap() panics too, turning one bad registration into a process-wide failure; use parking_lot, catch_unwind, or recover from poisoning explicitly.
Never hold the write guard across arbitrary user code (factory invocation, plugin callbacks): it deadlocks re-entrant registration and stalls all readers.
Entries live for the whole program - a registry that stores handles or instances pins them forever (no eviction); store factories, not instances, when lifetime matters.

variants.name: inventory crate (link-time distributed slice)
variants.implementation_notes: Registration without runtime locking: inventory::collect!(T) declares the registry type and inventory::submit!(expr) entries run as life-before-main initializers, so iterating inventory::iter::<T> yields &'static entries with no map, no lock and no duplicate policy. The classic structure survives only as the collected type plus the iteration site.
pitfalls: Registration runs as life-before-main, which is not available on every target (embedded, some no_std and sandboxed configurations) and confuses readers who expect main() to be the entry point.
Linkers can drop or duplicate submissions in static-library and -C link-dead-code builds; inventory's own docs point at linkme for a life-before-main-free approach.
Lookup is a linear scan over &'static entries with no duplicate detection; the table cannot change at runtime.

variants.name: TypeId-keyed type registry
variants.implementation_notes: When the key is the service type rather than a name, key a OnceLock<RwLock<HashMap<TypeId, Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync>>>> by TypeId::of::<T>() and downcast on lookup - this is how Rust DI-style containers and dynamic extension points model 'resolve T'. It trades compile-time safety for runtime type erasure and needs one registration per type.
pitfalls: TypeId is opaque and only comparable within one compilation: keys are not stable across crates built with different compiler versions, so exported or serialized ids must not be persisted.
Every value must be Send + Sync + 'static to go into the shared map, and downcast_ref silently returns None on a type mismatch unless you check.
A type-keyed registry cannot express two implementations of one trait: the key is the concrete type, so trait-object lookup needs a wrapper newtype or a name key.
